why: Threat-focused thoughts can add distress and make activity decisions harder. Noticing them is a skill—not evidence that pain is imagined.

slides.title: Pain and Thoughts Interact
slides.content: Pain can pull attention toward worst-case predictions. Those thoughts are understandable and can influence distress, confidence, and behaviour.

slides.title: Common Patterns
slides.content: Rumination, magnifying what a symptom might mean, and feeling helpless are sometimes grouped under the term pain catastrophizing.

slides.title: Not Blame
slides.content: These patterns do not cause every pain problem and are not a personal failure. Physical, psychological, and social factors can interact in different ways.

slides.title: Create Some Distance
slides.content: Try naming a thought—‘I am having the thought that…’—then choose the next useful action based on your goals and current situation.

slides.title: Get Support When Needed
slides.content: A trained clinician can help with persistent worry, distress, or avoidance. Psychological support is part of whole-person care, not a dismissal of symptoms.
